newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Estimate of world sugar balance.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Estimate of world sugar balance.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician
F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to
FIRST ESTIMATE OF THE WORLD SUGAR BALANCE 1996/97 -

1995/96 was a difficult year for sugar analysts. Despite a hefty sugar surplus the price did not collapse as some had predicted. There were various reasons for this. The availability of non-refined white sugar whose price is not reflected in official London or Paris market quotations was one of these, but the greatest reason was the fact that nearly 50 per cent of the surplus stock, which at the end of the year amounted to 9.1 million tonnes, was locked up in India. This cannot be discounted, it will not just disappear, but all the time that for political and infrastructural reasons this sugar cannot be exported, its market effect is muted.

A somewhat different situation will prevail in 1996/97. Consumption is expected to rise by 2.4 percent to about 120 million tonnes. However, even though the sharp rise in production seen in the past two seasons will come to a halt with output falling from 1995/96, it will still amount to around 124.0 million tonnes. There are a number of reasons why this figure differs from our recent forecast of production in crop year 1996/97, incidentally. In the first place these statistics are produced strictly on a September/August basis. Consequently in some cases, as for instance Brazil, the early months of the crop year 1996/97 are excluded while the corresponding early months of crop year 1997/98 are included.

In 1997/98 several countries will probably produce lower crops, one reason for the lower 1996/97 September/August year figure. Other factors are the probability of a lower crop in Cuba as a consequence of Hurricane Lili, the likelihood of a lower than expected crop in Thailand following heavy rains and lower than expected production in Pakistan because of increased diversion of cane to the gur producers.

Even after taking into consideration about one million tonnes of unrecorded disappearance that points to a further substantial hoist to world stocks with the stock/consumption ratio rising to 42.27 percent from 40.39 percent and less than 28 percent at the end of the 1980s. Meanwhile surplus stocks are forecast to rise to 10.6 million tonnes. The fact that India's share of the stocks is expected to fall to 43 percent indicates a build up in other areas and that could have a sharp impact on prices, as the holders of this sugar would probably not wish to hold it off the market. For that matter it also seems likely that exports from India will also rise during 1996/97, if markets can be found.

It appears that the white sugar side of the market has most reason for concern. Not only is import demand in the developing countries likely to fall - and it is these countries which mainly import white sugar - but in Europe Turkey and ex-Yugoslavia will need much less while the Russian government has taken active steps to deter white sugar imports by raising taxes and duties. But over and above all this will be the effect of the new refineries in the Middle East. The one in Dubai is already operating while commercial production is expected to commence at the Jeddah plant in the first quarter of 1997. These refineries will have a capacity in excess of one million tonnes and as they will produce high quality sugar of European standard it will presumably be the EU producers, China and to an extent the US in-transit refiners who will feel the brunt of their impact.

One welcome sign from the USA is that imports of raws for refining for the domestic market are expected to increase. If there is a bright spot in the white sugar market it may be that the financial problems associated with the massive output in India will eventually bring their own solution with a drop in production.

The outlook for the raws market looks to be less bleak. Demand will remain at around last year's level of more than 19 million tonnes. However, there is no reason to believe supplies will not be completely adequate to meet this requirement unless there are some unforeseen calamities.

Are there any reasons for optimism? The upward trend in production appears to have come to an end. Meanwhile a healthy increase in consumption is in prospect. These are welcome signs but the enormous stocks overhanging the market must not be overlooked.
